title-group.article-title: A Feasibility Study of the Repurposing of Prazosin to Improve Treatment Outcomes in Men Receiving Radiotherapy for Prostate Cancer (MiniRaP‐00)

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Further work is needed to improve treatment outcomes for prostate cancer (PCa), with the repurposing of the α1‐adrenoreceptor antagonists presenting a potential solution. This feasibility clinical trial presents the first prospective data of the use of an α1‐adrenoreceptor antagonist in men undergoing radiotherapy for PCa.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: The study enrolled men planned to receive radiotherapy for PCa. Participants received escalating doses of prazosin administered during radiotherapy. Blood pressure was recorded at each radiotherapy fraction. The primary outcome was treatment protocol feasibility and secondary outcomes were maximum tolerated dose (MTD) of prazosin, safety, and progression‐free survival (PFS).

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Ten participants were enrolled into the study and all achieved > 90% treatment compliance and > 80% assessment compliance. One participant and four participants achieved an MTD of 1 mg and 0.5 mg, respectively, and the remaining five participants had an MTD of 0 mg, with the overall protocol defined MTD being 0 mg. There were no Grades 3/4 adverse events. All treatment‐related adverse events (TRAE) were either hypotension or orthostatic hypotension, of the 17 reported TRAEs 16 were asymptomatic. No participants had evidence of disease progression at the 36‐week follow‐up.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Our study demonstrated that coadministration of prazosin during radiotherapy is feasible. However, the incidence of hypotension resulted in a protocol‐defined MTD (under conservative blood pressure based DLT definition) of 0 mg, although 16 of the 17 reports were asymptomatic. Combined with monitoring used in other studies utilizing prazosin, this suggests that our safety monitoring and dose‐limiting toxicity (DLT) definition may have been too strict and did not accurately reflect a clinically relevant MTD. As this study achieved its primary aim and demonstrated the feasibility of the administration of prazosin during radiotherapy, further prospective studies are justified, with greater consideration given to the definition of DLTs.

sec.p: Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry (381954).

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Prostate cancer (PCa) is the second most commonly diagnosed cancer and the fifth leading cause of cancer‐related death in men worldwide [1]. With the 5‐year survival rate of PCa approaching 100%, however, upon progression to metastatic disease, 5‐year survival drops to 37% [2]. Due to the high prevalence and poor prognosis upon disease progression, further research is needed to improve the outcomes of PCa treatments.

With the time and cost challenges associated with novel drug development, drug repurposing provides an efficient and cost‐effective option to address this problem. Drug repurposing is a strategy that utilizes existing drugs, which have received regulatory approval for non‐cancer indications in the treatment of cancer [3, 4]. In recent years, drug repurposing has gained further attention due to the reduced financial and time burdens compared to novel drug development. Furthermore, it provides a lower risk profile due to the known pharmacokinetic, pharmacodynamic, and safety profiles of the target drug [5]. The α1‐adrenoreceptor antagonist drug class has attracted attention as a candidate for repurposing in PCa [6]. Several other agents, including aspirin, statins, and metformin, have been identified as promising drug repurposing candidates promoting cancer radiosensitization [7].

The α1‐adrenoreceptor antagonist drug class contains several drugs with differing structures. Those with quinazoline‐based structures include prazosin, terazosin, and doxazosin, with these displaying nonselective actions toward the α1‐adrenoreceptor subtypes. In contrast, the sulfonamide derivative, tamsulosin, displays uroselectivity via the α1A‐adrenoreceptor [8]. Past research has demonstrated the anticancer properties of prazosin, doxazosin, and terazosin in both hormone‐sensitive (LNCaP and DU‐145) and hormone‐resistant (PC‐3) PCa cell lines in vitro and in murine models [9, 10, 11, 12]. Importantly, these anticancer properties are found to be specific to the quinazoline‐based derivatives and not the sulfonamide‐based tamsulosin [9]. Furthermore, treatment with quinazoline‐based α1‐adrenoreceptor antagonists has been found to increase the sensitivity of PCa cells to ionizing radiation [13]. Various mechanisms have been attributed to the anticancer properties of quinazoline‐based α1‐adrenoreceptor antagonists. These include the upregulation of pro‐apoptotic mediators such as caspase‐3, caspase‐8, TGF‐β, and p53, and the downregulation of focal adhesion kinase, epidermal growth factor receptor, topoisomerase‐1, and Akt/mTOR [8]. Prazosin was selected as the study treatment due to being the only available quinazoline α1‐adrenoreceptor antagonist in Australia.

Despite the evidence revealed by in vitro and murine models, published data on the cytotoxic or radiosensitizing potential of quinazoline‐based α1‐adrenoreceptor antagonists on PCa in humans are limited. Past literature suggests a lower incidence of PCa in men that were treated with either doxazosin or terazosin [14] and that terazosin, independently of radiotherapy, may result in a significant reduction in prostate microvessel density, an important feature of PCa tumor growth and survival [15].

Currently, to our knowledge there is only one available study investigating the impacts of α1‐adrenoreceptor antagonists on radiotherapy in a human population [16], however, this was a retrospective analysis of patients taking α1‐adrenoreceptor antagonists for non‐cancer related purposes. The study suggested that prazosin delays time to relapse and increases survival in men with localized PCa treated with radiotherapy. At the 5‐year time point only 8.8% of patients who were taking prazosin at the time of radiotherapy had displayed biochemical relapse, which was significantly (p < 0.001) lower than the control (34.5%). Prazosin was also found to significantly (p < 0.0001) increase recurrence‐free survival compared to the control group [16].

In this open‐label feasibility study, we aimed to provide the first prospective evidence of the feasibility, safety, and maximum tolerated dose (MTD) of prazosin, an α1‐adrenoreceptor antagonist, when taken as an adjunct to radiotherapy. In addition, we looked at progression‐free survival (PFS) at 36 weeks posttreatment. The findings from this study will be used to guide future efficacy studies.

sec.title: Study Design
sec.p: The study was an open‐label feasibility clinical trial utilizing escalating doses of prazosin in men undergoing standard of care radiotherapy for PCa. The study received ethical approval from the Ramsay Health Care HREC A (2020/ETH/1032) and was registered on the Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry (381954).

Key inclusion criteria included histologically confirmed adenocarcinoma of the prostate, plan to receive a course of radiotherapy consisting of at least 20 fractions, age greater or equal to 18 years, normal liver and renal function, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status of 0 to 1 and willingness to comply with all study procedures including the prazosin administration protocol and assessments. Key exclusion criteria included evidence of > 5 metastatic sites, presence of any medical, psychological or social condition that may hinder compliance, use of hormonal therapy more than 30 days prior to commencement of prazosin other than for the treatment of PCa, history of any other invasive malignancy within 5 years of the commencement of prazosin other than successfully treated squamous cell or basal cell carcinoma of the skin, received prior brachytherapy or radiotherapy for PCa to the same site, planned treatment with stereotactic ablative body radiotherapy, pre‐existing hypotension, pre‐existing orthostatic hypotension, allergy to quinazolines, treatment with α1‐adrenoreceptor antagonists within the previous 6 months, planned cataract surgery, patients with high falls risk as assessed by the investigator and known gastrointestinal disease that could affect the absorption or tolerance of prazosin. A target sample size of 30 participants was determined for the study. Potential participants were identified by the investigator and provided information on the study. Following provision of informed consent, eligibility was determined by the investigator prior to enrolling the participant onto the study (Figure 1).

sec.title: Outcome Definitions
sec.p: Protocol and treatment compliance were defined as more than 90% of prazosin treatment doses taken and all radiotherapy fractions completed, and at least 80% of the assessments completed in accordance with the protocol. MTD was originally defined as the highest dose reached in each individual participant where there was an absence of dose‐limiting toxicities (DLTs) or to the maximum dose of 5 mg twice daily in the absence of any DLTs. After the first three participants, the trial design was altered to a standard 3 + 3 dose escalation design, so the MTD definition was changed to the highest dose cohort which was completed. Safety was reported as the incidence of adverse events, with radiotherapy‐related adverse events graded using the RTOG/EORTC Acute and Late Radiation Morbidity Scoring Schema and all other adverse events graded using the Clinical Terminology for Adverse Events (CTCAE) v5.0. Treatment‐related adverse events (TRAEs) were defined as adverse events deemed to be either possibly or probably related to prazosin by the investigator. DLT was defined as a ≥ 20 mmHg drop in systolic blood pressure (SBP) or ≥ 10 mmHg drop in diastolic blood pressure (DBP) between lying and standing, a blood pressure reading of < 100 mmHg SBP or < 70 mmHg DBP or a Grade 2 or higher toxicity, as per CTCAE v5.0, deemed to be caused by prazosin during treatment.

Clinical or biochemical PFS was defined as the time from the start of prazosin to the date of first clinical or biochemical evidence of disease progression or recurrence or death from any cause, whichever comes first. Biochemical progression was defined as a PSA rise ≥ 2 ng/mL above the PSA nadir for definitive radiotherapy and a PSA rise > 0.4 ng/mL for salvage radiotherapy following prostatectomy [17, 18]. Due to the target participant population and short duration of the follow‐up period, this outcome is descriptive only and was not used to determine conclusions on efficacy.

sec.title: Treatment
sec.p: The original study design was that of an intra‐participant dose escalation. In the first three participants, prazosin was to be administered orally in escalating doses from 0.5 mg twice daily to a maximum of 5 mg twice daily, commencing 1 week prior to radiotherapy. The dose was increased to 1 mg twice daily at the commencement of radiotherapy and then escalated by 1 mg each week until an MTD or 5 mg twice daily was reached.

Following a decision by the Trial Management Committee, a 3 + 3 dose escalation design was utilized for the remaining seven participants. The change was made due to poor tolerability of prazosin during the intra‐participant dose escalation design resulting in all three participants having to discontinue treatment due to the presence of DLTs. DLTs persisted in all three participants despite dose reductions, therefore, a 3 + 3 design was utilized to determine if DLTs occurred at all dose levels or only once escalated beyond a certain dose.

During the 3 + 3 phase, three participants were enrolled to escalating dose levels of prazosin (0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 mg) administered orally twice daily. Prazosin was to commence 1 week prior to radiotherapy and cease upon completion of radiotherapy. As per a standard 3 + 3 design, three participants were enrolled to each dose level, starting at the lowest dose. If there were no DLTs at the respective dose level, the study proceeded to the next level. If one participant developed a DLT then an additional three participants were enrolled into the same dose level, should a second participant develop at DLT at the same level then the previous dose level was defined as the MTD. The MTD or 5 mg BD, whichever is reached first, was then planned to be taken forward into dose expansion to a total of 30 participants across all dose levels for the trial, see Figure 2.

caption.p: Standard 3 + 3 dose escalation and dose expansion schema. BD = twice daily; DL = dose level; MTD = maximum tolerated dose. [Color figure can be viewed at wileyonlinelibrary.com]

sec.p: After each dose level cohort was completed, safety data were reviewed by the Trial Management Committee prior to the next cohort being opened for enrollment. Due to the known adverse event profile of prazosin and as per prescribing guidance, it was necessary to titrate the dose up to the target level. All participants were commenced on 0.5 mg twice daily, with the dose increased to 1 mg twice daily after 1 week and increased by 1 mg twice daily each week until the target dose for the respective cohort was reached or a DLT occurred. In the event of a DLT, the dose was returned to the previous dosing level and not escalated further. If the DLT persisted, the dose level could be de‐escalated by another dose level. If, after two de‐escalations or due to the severity of the initial DLT, as determined by the investigator, prazosin was ceased. Concomitant antihypertensive medications were not modified or withheld during dose escalation, as these medications were managed by treating teams not involved in the study.

All participants received standard of care conventional radiotherapy as per local guidelines. All radiotherapy treatments were delivered using volumetric modulated arc therapy (VMAT) with daily image guidance consisting of cone beam computed tomography scans. The VMAT utilized 6 MV beams delivered by a linear accelerator. Treatments were administered daily on weekdays with total dose ranging from 60 to 66 Gy divided over 20–33 fractions depending on participants' individual disease.
The use of ADT was not defined as part of the study and was used at the discretion of the treating oncologist.

sec.title: Assessments
sec.p: All participants had baseline assessments to ensure they met all of the inclusion criteria and none of the exclusion criteria. During the study, all participants underwent lying and standing blood pressure readings with each fraction of radiotherapy. Participants were asked to lay down and a reading taken after 5 min. Participants were then asked to stand and another reading was taken after 1–3 min. Readings were not taken at specific time intervals from prazosin dosing.

At weekly intervals, compliance and clinical assessments were carried out by the investigator. All other assessments were conducted as per local procedures for radiotherapy treatment of PCa. Participants entered safety follow‐up for 36 weeks after the last fraction of radiotherapy. All adverse events occurring within 30 days of the completion of prazosin were graded as per the CTCAE v5.0 and assessed for causality to prazosin. Follow‐up visits occurred at 12, 24, and 36 weeks after the completion of radiotherapy and radiotherapy‐related adverse events graded as per the RTOG/EORTC Late Radiation Morbidity Scoring Schema.

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: Descriptive statistics were used to present the findings of the study. Categorical data are displayed in the tables as numbers and percentages. Continuous variables are reported as medians and ranges. As no between group comparisons were conducted, no formal statistical tests were performed.

sec.title: Study Population
sec.p: The investigators identified 11 potential participants between October 21, 2022 and June 4, 2024, with 10 providing informed consent and being enrolled onto the study. All 10 participants met all the inclusion criteria and none of the exclusion criteria. While the target sample size was 30 participants, due to the incidence of DLTs the study was terminated early. The decision to terminate the study early was made by the Trial Management Committee who met on a fortnightly basis during the study period.

Six participants received definitive radiotherapy for locoregional disease, with none being considered low‐risk, five intermediate risk and one high risk. Three participants were being treated with salvage radiotherapy following relapse post‐RP and one with radiotherapy for oligometastatic disease. Six participants had prior prostate surgery either via RP or transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP). Of note, seven participants had pre‐existing hypertension and eight were taking antihypertension medications, see Table S1 for further detail. Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics of the participants are displayed in Table 1.

sec.title: Treatment and Assessment Compliance
sec.p: All 10 participants achieved > 90% overall treatment compliance. Seven participants achieved 100% compliance with the prazosin treatment protocol and all participants received all planned radiotherapy fractions.

Overall assessment compliance was > 80% for all participants. When categorized into the different stages of the trial (screening, treatment, and follow‐up), compliance rates remained above 80% for all participants. Assessment compliance of 100% was achieved for six participants. Across all participants, 350 of 352 (99%) protocol blood pressure readings were completed.

sec.title: Maximum Tolerated Dose (MTD)
sec.p: Five participants had a MTD of 0 mg, four of 0.5 mg, and one of 1 mg (Table 2). At the completion of the 3 + 3 dose escalation phase, the overall MTD was determined to be 0 mg and the dose expansion phase was abandoned.

fn.p: Participants 01T, 02T, and 03T were enrolled to weekly escalating doses before the study protocol was amended to a 3 + 3 design.

sec.p: The first three participants who were enrolled to receive weekly escalating doses all had a MTD of 0 mg. Participants 01T and 02T both reached a dose of 1 mg before experiencing a DLT requiring dose de‐escalation to 0.5 mg and a further DLT resulting in an MTD of 0 mg. Participant 03T reached a dose of 2 mg before experiencing a DLT, with further DLTs at 1 and 0.5 mg doses resulting in a DLT of 0 mg.

During the 3 + 3 design phase, all three participants completed the 0.5 mg dose cohort. However, of the participants assigned to the 1 mg cohort, 07T was dose reduced to 0.5 mg due to a DLT, 08T completed the 1 mg dosing, and the third participant, 09T, did not complete treatment due to DLTs during the 0.5 mg dose titration week.

Prior to confirming the trial MTD of 0.5 mg, the Trial Management Committee decided that as participant 09T had a MTD of 0 mg one additional participant should be enrolled into the 0.5 mg dose cohort to confirm safety of this dose level prior to dose expansion. The final participant, 10T, was unable to complete treatment at 0.5 mg due to a DLT, therefore, the trial management committee confirmed the MTD for the trial to be 0 mg and to terminate the study (Figure 3).

sec.title: Adverse Events
sec.p: Nine of the participants (90%) reported at least one adverse event (AE) during treatment or within 30 days of completing prazosin. TRAEs occurred in six participants, all of the TRAEs were either hypotension or orthostatic hypotension. Rates of hypotension and orthostatic hypotension were 40% and 30%, respectively, with a total of 12 hypotension events and 5 orthostatic hypotension events. There were no Grades 3 or 4 adverse events. One participant reported symptomatic hypotension, with 16 of the 17 reported incidences of hypotension and orthostatic hypotension being asymptomatic.
Table 3 outlines adverse events during treatment and within 30‐day safety follow‐up period.

When focusing on protocol defined DLTs, there were a total of 6 (60%) participants that experienced a DLT, with a total number of 17 DLTs across these 6 participants. When applying a clinically relevant DLT definition of symptomatic hypotension and/or any adverse event ≥ Grade 2 as per the CTCAE, there was one participant (10%) that had a DLT and one DLT event. Table 4 outlines the protocol defined and clinically relevant defined DLTs per participant.

sec.p: At the 12‐week follow‐up, three participants reported adverse events (Table 5). These adverse events were erectile dysfunction, hot flushes, and COVID‐19 infection. No Grades 3 or 4 adverse events were reported.

sec.title: Clinical or Biochemical Progression‐Free Survival
sec.p: No participants had clinical or chemical evidence of disease progression or recurrence and all participants were still alive at the completion of the follow‐up period. Follow‐up PSA values demonstrated no evidence of biochemical recurrence (Table 6).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: With the high prevalence of PCa and the poor prognosis following progression from early stage to metastatic disease, there is a need to improve current available treatments. As the introduction of novel agents into the market is both costly and time‐consuming, drug repurposing may provide a more efficient approach to finding new cancer treatments. This study presented the first prospective human data into the re‐purposing of the α1‐adrenoreceptor antagonist prazosin for the use in PCa.

The primary outcome of the study was to demonstrate the feasibility, based on treatment and assessment compliance, of the proposed protocol of coadministration of prazosin during radiotherapy for PCa. According to the definition of treatment and assessment compliance, it was demonstrated that twice daily prazosin administration commencing 1 week prior to, and continuing until the completion of radiotherapy, unless ceased early due to toxicity, was feasible. High treatment compliance was believed to be associated with the ease of dosing. Prazosin is taken orally, twice daily, irrespective of food, allowing dosing to fit easily into a person's daily routine. Furthermore, many of the assessments conducted in this trial formed part of the standard‐of‐care approach for men being treated with radiotherapy for PCa. This may have contributed to the high rates of assessment compliance.

Although the study demonstrated feasibility of the proposed protocol, it also found an MTD of 0 mg, when analyzed using the protocol defined DLT definition, due to the incidence of hypotension and orthostatic hypotension. The α1‐adrenoreceptors play a key role in smooth muscle contraction including both vascular and prostate smooth muscle [19]. Due to prazosin's high affinity for all three α1‐adrenoreceptor subtypes (α1A, α1B, and α1D), both hypotension and orthostatic hypotension are known adverse effects of the drug [20]. This is in comparison to the uroselective α1‐adrenoreceptor antagonists, such as tamsulosin, which show selectivity for the α1A adrenoreceptors and demonstrate a lower risk of vascular‐related adverse events [21].

Due to the known adverse effect profile of prazosin and risk factors, such as age > 65 years [22], hypotension and orthostatic hypotension were considered adverse events of interest and additional monitoring put in place during the study. The incidence of hypotension and orthostatic hypotension, 40% and 30%, respectively, were found to be higher in our study than other studies utilizing prazosin as the investigational agent. Aubin and colleagues conducted a study in individuals with alcohol use disorder and reported an orthostatic hypotension incidence of 7.4% at a 5 mg daily dose and 4.3% at 10 mg daily [23]. This study had a larger sample size of 54 and 46 in each of the two dosing groups and significantly lower participant mean age of 49.1 and 51.8 years in each group. Wang and colleagues conducted a study in patients with Alzheimer's disease and reported a hypotension incidence rate of 18% [24]. This study had a similar sample size with 11 participants receiving prazosin and a higher mean age of 83.2 years. Of note, the mean baseline standing systolic and DBPs of these two studies were 138/88 and 134/75 mmHg, respectively, both being lower than those reported in our study, 160/86 mmHg. Furthermore, our participant population had a hypertension incidence rate of 70%; however, this was not reported in either of the previously mentioned studies. These findings combined with past evidence that patients with hypertension tend to have a more pronounced blood pressure reductions on commencement of prazosin [21] suggest that the higher incidence of hypotension and orthostatic hypotension might be due to the varied baseline blood pressure and high hypertension rates in our participant population.

In our study, lying and standing blood pressure were monitored with each fraction of radiotherapy, which were then used to determine the presence of DLTs. This resulted in readings being taken every weekday during radiotherapy treatment. This is in comparison to other studies that have utilized weekly or twice weekly monitoring [23, 25]. Furthermore, many studies investigating prazosin report subjective measures of hypotension and orthostatic hypotension such as dizziness on standing and lightheadedness, rather than objective measures such as change in blood pressure [26, 27, 28]. In our study, of the 17 reports of hypotension or orthostatic hypotension, 16 were asymptomatic (Grade 1) and one was of symptomatic (Grade 2), corresponding to a 10% incidence rate of symptomatic hypotension/orthostatic hypotension, aligning more closely with other studies using prazosin [23]. The differences in rates of reported versus symptomatic hypotension/orthostatic hypotension in our study, when combined with the frequency of monitoring, may suggest our safety monitoring protocol and protocol‐defined DLTs were overly cautious and did not accurately report adverse events that were of clinical significance. This finding presents a key learning for future study development.

Furthermore, when applying a clinically relevant DLT definition of symptomatic hypotension and/or any adverse event ≥ Grade 2 as per the CTCAE, this would have reduced the number of DLTs from 17 to 1. When using this clinically relevant definition, the single DLT occurred in participant 09T, which highlights the possibility of unnecessary termination of early dose cohorts, however, further studies would be required to confirm this.

Due to the absence of any prospective data in humans being treated with prazosin for cancer and while undergoing radiotherapy treatment, the impact of using prazosin in cancer patients and during radiotherapy on the vascular system cannot be ruled out. A study by Iwanski and colleagues concluded that cancer is a significant and independent predictor of orthostatic hypotension [29]. Furthermore, past evidence has suggested that radiotherapy being used in the treatment of cancer has the ability to reduce blood pressure [30]. More recently, Leibowitz and colleagues conducted a study that concluded that radiotherapy for head and neck cancer resulted in sustained blood pressure reductions but no impact on orthostatic hypotension, however, it is not clear whether these findings would also be true for patients with PCa due to the significant anatomical differences between these regions, notably the presence of baroreceptors in the neck [31].

Finally, while the study reported that no participants met the definition of disease progression, this is not unexpected due to the high 5‐year survival rates in this participant population [2]. Furthermore, due to the heterogeneity of the participant population, small sample size, and short duration of the follow‐up period, the PFS outcome is simply descriptive and does not provide any indication of the efficacy of prazosin administration during radiotherapy for PCa. Further prospective studies that are suitably powered are required to determine the efficacy of this combination.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This study presents the first prospective human data of the use of the α1‐adrenoreceptor antagonist prazosin as an adjunct to radiotherapy for PCa. The study achieved the primary outcome of demonstrating the feasibility of the prazosin dosing regimen. However, the incidence of DLTs limited dose escalation and resulted in early termination of the study, with the protocol‐defined MTD (under conservative blood pressure based DLT criteria) being 0 mg. However, this was largely down the overly strict protocol DLT definition with 16 of the 17 reports of hypotensive events being asymptomatic. Future studies are warranted and should consider concomitant treatment with antihypertensive medications, pre‐existing hypertension when developing inclusion/exclusion criteria and the use of subjective measurements when defining DLTs.
